title: Venus–Jupiter “cosmic kiss” conjunction
shortDescription: Venus and Jupiter will appear extremely close together in the evening sky, creating a brilliant pair brighter than any star.
mainDescription: For a brief evening on June 9, 2026, Venus and Jupiter will appear remarkably close together in the twilight sky. Shortly after sunset, the two brightest planets visible from Earth will align low above the western horizon, separated by only about 1.6 degrees — close enough to resemble a brilliant double star to the naked eye. Although the planets remain hundreds of millions of kilometers apart in space, their alignment from Earth’s perspective will create one of the most striking planetary conjunctions visible without a telescope. Venus will shine with a steady white brilliance, while Jupiter glows nearby against the fading light of dusk. Events like this have drawn the attention of skywatchers for centuries, combining the precision of celestial mechanics with a rare moment of visual beauty in the night sky.
whatYoullSee: A bright double “star” low in the evening sky, shining far brighter than anything else around it.
whyItMatters: This is one of the most visually impressive and easily observable planetary alignments visible to the naked eye.
keyFacts: Two brightest planets in the sky
Visible to the naked eye even from cities
nextOccurrences: Next bright Venus-Jupiter conjunctions are expected in the early 2030s. Similar spectacular pairings occur roughly every 10–13 years.

title: Greatest solar eclipse (Europe)
shortDescription: A total solar eclipse will cross parts of Europe, bringing up to 2 minutes and 18 seconds of totality.
mainDescription: On August 12, 2026, the Moon’s shadow will sweep across the Arctic, Iceland, northern Spain, and parts of Portugal, bringing the first total solar eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999. For a few brief minutes along the path of totality, the Sun will disappear completely behind the Moon, turning daytime into an eerie twilight. Observers will be able to see the Sun’s outer atmosphere — the glowing solar corona — while bright planets and stars emerge in the darkened sky. At the point of greatest eclipse near Iceland, totality will last up to 2 minutes and 18 seconds. Because the eclipse crosses populated and easily accessible regions of Europe, it is expected to become one of the most widely observed astronomical events of the decade. In northern Spain especially, the eclipse will occur low above the horizon near sunset, creating an especially unusual and dramatic view.
whatYoullSee: The Sun fully covered by the Moon, a glowing white corona, sudden twilight in the middle of the day, and bright stars or planets in the darkened sky.
whyItMatters: It is one of the best total solar eclipses visible from Europe in many years and offers an excellent opportunity for both public viewing and scientific study.
keyFacts: Path crosses Iceland, northern Spain, and Portugal
First total solar eclipse in mainland Europe since 1999
nextOccurrences: Next major total solar eclipse with good European visibility: September 3, 2081
Other total solar eclipses will occur in different parts of the world in the coming decades.

title: 99942 Apophis close flyby
shortDescription: Asteroid Apophis will pass extremely close to Earth — closer than many satellites — and may be visible to the naked eye as a moving star.
mainDescription: Asteroid 99942 Apophis will make one of the closest known flybys of a large asteroid in recorded history. Passing only about 31,600 kilometers above Earth’s surface — closer than many geostationary satellites — Apophis will become visible to the naked eye across parts of Europe, Africa, and Asia. As it races past Earth, observers will be able to notice its motion across the sky in real time, something rarely visible with an asteroid of this size. Once considered a possible impact threat after its discovery in 2004, Apophis is now known to pose no danger to Earth. Instead, the encounter will give scientists a rare opportunity to study how Earth’s gravity can alter an asteroid’s orbit, rotation, and surface structure during an extremely close flyby.
whatYoullSee: A fast-moving point of light crossing the night sky, visible to the naked eye under dark skies as a star-like object that shifts position over minutes.
whyItMatters: It is one of the closest approaches of a sizable asteroid in recorded history and a major event for both astronomy and planetary defense studies.
keyFacts: Closest approach: ~31,600 km from Earth’s surface
Visible to the naked eye in dark skies
Best viewed from Europe, Africa, and western Asia
nextOccurrences: Apophis will not make another close approach like this for over 100 years. The next significant close pass is expected in 2060, but much farther away.

title: Taurid meteor swarm (fireball years)
shortDescription: Earth will pass through a dense part of the Taurid meteor stream, producing many bright fireballs.
mainDescription: Earth is expected to pass through an unusually dense region of the Taurid meteor complex in late 2032, increasing the chances of seeing bright fireballs streak across the night sky. Unlike most meteor showers, which are known for producing many small and fast meteors, the Taurids are famous for their slow-moving, exceptionally bright fireballs. Some can shine brighter than the planets and remain visible for several seconds as they cross the sky. During enhanced Taurid years — sometimes called “Fireball Years” — this activity becomes noticeably more intense. The elevated meteor activity may continue for several weeks, giving observers multiple opportunities to witness unusually dramatic meteors under dark skies away from city lights. While the Taurids rarely produce large numbers of meteors at once, they are considered one of the best meteor showers for visible fireballs and persistent glowing trails.
whatYoullSee: Slow, bright fireballs streaking across the sky, some lasting several seconds and leaving glowing trains.
whyItMatters: This is one of the best opportunities in the 2030s to see numerous bright fireballs from a single meteor complex.
keyFacts: Meteors are slow but often very bright
Best observed after midnight in dark skies
nextOccurrences: The next strong Taurid fireball years are expected around 2040 and then again in the 2050s.
Normal Taurid activity occurs every year in October and November, but 2032 is predicted to be significantly stronger.

title: Blood moon tetrad
shortDescription: Four total lunar eclipses (Blood Moons) will occur in a row over 18 months — a rare lunar tetrad.
mainDescription: A rare sequence of four consecutive total lunar eclipses will unfold between April 2032 and October 2033, creating what astronomers call a lunar tetrad. During each eclipse, the Moon will pass completely through Earth’s shadow and take on a deep red or copper glow — the result of sunlight being filtered through Earth’s atmosphere before reaching the lunar surface. The effect, often called a “Blood Moon,” can make the Moon appear unusually dark, dim, and dramatic against the night sky. Lunar tetrads occur only a few times per century, and all four eclipses in this series will be visible from large regions of Earth. Unlike solar eclipses, total lunar eclipses can be observed safely with the naked eye and unfold slowly over several hours, making them among the most accessible astronomical events for skywatchers worldwide.
whatYoullSee: The Moon gradually darkening and turning copper-red during totality, lasting up to nearly two hours per eclipse.
whyItMatters: A Blood Moon Tetrad is a striking and memorable series that captures public attention and provides excellent opportunities for skywatchers.
keyFacts: Four total lunar eclipses in 18 months
Visible from large portions of Earth
Safe to watch with the naked eye
nextOccurrences: The next lunar tetrad after 2032–2033 will occur in 2043–2044.
Lunar tetrads happen only a few times every century.

title: Great planetary alignment
shortDescription: Several bright planets will line up across the sky in a spectacular planetary parade.
mainDescription: Several of the Solar System’s brightest planets will appear together in the sky during a rare planetary alignment in September 2034. Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are expected to line up along the ecliptic — the apparent path the Sun follows across the sky — creating what is often called a “planet parade.” Although the planets will remain separated by vast distances in space, their positions from Earth’s perspective will place them across the same region of the sky in a striking celestial arrangement. Planetary alignments involving five bright naked-eye planets are relatively uncommon and have attracted attention for centuries. For observers with clear skies, the event will offer an unusually broad view of the Solar System’s architecture, with multiple worlds visible at the same time without the need for a telescope.
whatYoullSee: Five or more bright planets visible at once, lined up like beads on a string across the sky.
whyItMatters: Great planetary alignments are visually impressive and generate widespread public interest in astronomy.
keyFacts: Best observed from dark or semi-dark locations
Occurs roughly every 10–20 years for strong alignments
nextOccurrences: The next strong planetary alignment is expected around 2040.
Smaller alignments of 3–4 planets occur more frequently, every few years.

title: Great Mars opposition
shortDescription: Mars will reach its closest approach to Earth, appearing exceptionally bright and large in the night sky.
mainDescription: Mars will reach one of its most favorable oppositions of the coming decades, appearing brighter and larger in Earth’s sky than it normally does. During opposition, Earth passes between Mars and the Sun, placing the two planets on the same side of the Solar System and bringing Mars unusually close to Earth. In 2035, the distance between the planets will shrink to about 56 million kilometers, allowing Mars to shine at an impressive magnitude of around −2.8. To the naked eye, Mars will stand out as a vivid orange-red object dominating the night sky. Through small telescopes, observers may be able to distinguish dark surface markings, bright polar caps, and changes in atmospheric conditions on the planet itself. Because especially close oppositions occur only every 15 to 17 years, this event is expected to become one of the best opportunities of the next two decades for amateur astronomers to observe the Red Planet in detail.
whatYoullSee: A very bright orange-red “star” that outshines most other planets, with visible surface details in a telescope.
whyItMatters: Close Mars oppositions like this offer excellent opportunities for both casual viewing and serious astronomical observation.
nextOccurrences: The next similarly close Mars opposition will occur in 2041.
Mars reaches opposition roughly every 26 months, but truly great ones happen less frequently.

title: Extreme supermoon
shortDescription: One of the closest and brightest full Moons of the decade, appearing significantly larger and brighter than average.
mainDescription: The full Moon of November 2037 will coincide almost perfectly with the Moon’s closest approach to Earth, creating one of the most pronounced supermoons of the decade. As the Moon reaches perigee — the nearest point in its orbit around Earth — it will appear noticeably larger and brighter than a typical full Moon. Under ideal conditions, the difference may reach up to 14% in apparent size and around 30% in brightness compared to a more distant full Moon. The effect is often most striking near the horizon, where the Moon can appear unusually massive against landscapes and city skylines. While supermoons occur regularly, this particular event stands out because of the Moon’s exceptional proximity to Earth, making it one of the closest and brightest full Moons visible in the 2030s.
whatYoullSee: A noticeably larger and brighter full Moon, especially impressive when rising or setting near the horizon.
whyItMatters: Extreme supermoons create beautiful photo opportunities and help remind people to look up at the night sky.
keyFacts: One of the closest full Moons of the decade
Up to 14% larger and 30% brighter than average
Occurs when perigee and full Moon coincide closely
nextOccurrences: Extreme supermoons occur every few years when the Moon’s perigee is particularly close.
Regular supermoons happen several times each year.

title: Saturn ring plane crossing
shortDescription: Saturn’s famous rings will appear almost invisible as they align edge-on with Earth.
mainDescription: Saturn’s iconic rings will appear to almost vanish as the planet reaches a rare ring plane crossing in 2038. During this event, Earth will pass through the exact plane of Saturn’s rings, causing the enormous ring system to turn nearly edge-on from our perspective. Although the rings span hundreds of thousands of kilometers, they are remarkably thin relative to their width, making them difficult to see when viewed from the side. For a short period, Saturn will lose much of its familiar appearance and resemble a pale golden sphere crossed by a narrow line. Ring plane crossings occur only about once every 15 years and are especially valuable for astronomers, since the reduced glare from the rings can make Saturn’s moons and faint surrounding structures easier to observe. In the years following the crossing, the rings will gradually tilt open again and slowly regain their bright, dramatic appearance in Earth’s sky.
whatYoullSee: Saturn appearing as a plain oval disk with almost no visible rings — a rare and striking change from its usual appearance.
whyItMatters: This is one of the most interesting viewing angles of Saturn and helps astronomers study its ring dynamics.
keyFacts: Rings appear nearly invisible for several weeks
nextOccurrences: The next ring plane crossing after 2038 will occur around 2053.
This event repeats roughly every 15 years due to Saturn’s orbital tilt.

title: Greatest solar eclipse (North America)
shortDescription: One of the greatest total solar eclipses of the 21st century will cross the United States and Canada.
mainDescription: A major total solar eclipse will cross North America in 2045, bringing one of the longest and most accessible eclipses visible from the continent in the 21st century. Along the path of totality, the Moon will completely cover the Sun for up to 6 minutes and 6 seconds — an unusually long duration for a total solar eclipse. As daylight suddenly fades, observers will be able to see the Sun’s glowing corona surrounding the dark silhouette of the Moon, while bright planets and stars emerge in the darkened sky. The eclipse path is expected to pass through heavily populated regions stretching from the western United States to the Northeast, allowing millions of people to experience totality without traveling far. Because of its combination of long totality, favorable viewing conditions, and wide accessibility, this eclipse is widely expected to become one of the most significant astronomical events visible from North America in decades.
whatYoullSee: Complete darkness during the day, a brilliant solar corona, bright planets and stars visible in the sky, and a dramatic twilight on the horizon.
whyItMatters: This is one of the longest and most accessible total solar eclipses in North America for decades.
keyFacts: Path crosses the entire United States from west to east
Visible to tens of millions of people
nextOccurrences: The next total solar eclipse with similar long duration across North America is not expected until the 2070s.
Other total solar eclipses will occur in different parts of the world in the coming decades.

title: Brightest Jupiter of the century
shortDescription: Jupiter will reach its closest opposition of the century, appearing exceptionally bright and large.
mainDescription: Jupiter will make its closest approach to Earth of the mid-21st century, creating one of the finest viewing opportunities of the giant planet in decades. Shining at around magnitude −2.9, Jupiter will outshine every star in the night sky and become one of the brightest objects visible after sunset. At this unusually close distance, the planet’s disk will appear noticeably larger than during most oppositions, making details in its atmosphere easier to observe even through small telescopes. Observers with modest equipment may be able to see Jupiter’s cloud bands, the Great Red Spot, and the constant motion of its four largest moons — Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto — as they orbit the planet night after night. Favorable oppositions like this occur only when Jupiter is near the closer part of its orbit relative to Earth, making this one of the most impressive Jupiter apparitions for many years to come.
whatYoullSee: An incredibly bright planet with visible cloud bands and moons when viewed through a telescope.
whyItMatters: This is the best viewing conditions for Jupiter in the entire century.
keyFacts: Closest Jupiter opposition of the 21st century
Excellent for both naked-eye and telescopic observation
nextOccurrences: Jupiter reaches opposition every 13 months, but this is the closest and brightest one of the century.
The next very close opposition will occur much later in the 22nd century.

title: Halley’s Comet return
shortDescription: The most famous comet in history will return to the inner Solar System after 76 years.
mainDescription: Halley’s Comet will return to the inner Solar System for the first time since 1986, bringing back one of the most famous and historically significant objects in the night sky. As the comet approaches the Sun, solar radiation will heat its icy surface, releasing gas and dust that form a glowing coma and a long luminous tail stretching across space. Although the exact brightness of comets is difficult to predict far in advance, Halley’s Comet is expected to become visible to the naked eye for an extended period during its 2061 return. The comet has been observed and recorded for thousands of years, appearing in historical accounts from ancient civilizations to medieval Europe. Because Halley completes one orbit around the Sun roughly every 75 to 76 years, each return is effectively a once-in-a-lifetime event for most people — offering a rare connection between modern observers and generations who witnessed the same comet centuries ago.
whatYoullSee: A bright comet with a glowing head and a long tail stretching across the night sky under dark conditions.
whyItMatters: Halley’s Comet is the most famous periodic comet and connects modern observers with centuries of astronomical history.
keyFacts: May become visible to the naked eye
nextOccurrences: Halley’s Comet will return again in 2134.
After 2134, the next return is expected in 2209.

title: Greatest solar eclipse (Europe)
shortDescription: A major total solar eclipse will cross much of Europe with long duration of totality.
mainDescription: A major total solar eclipse will cross Europe in 2081, becoming one of the most significant eclipses visible from the continent in the second half of the 21st century. Along the path of totality, the Moon will completely cover the Sun for more than five minutes in some locations — an unusually long duration for a total solar eclipse. As the Sun disappears behind the Moon, daylight will fade into twilight, temperatures may briefly drop, and the Sun’s outer atmosphere, known as the corona, will become visible surrounding the dark lunar silhouette. Because the eclipse path is expected to pass through densely populated parts of Europe, millions of people will have an opportunity to experience totality without traveling far. The combination of long totality, broad visibility, and favorable viewing regions is expected to make this one of Europe’s most memorable astronomical events of the century.
whatYoullSee: The Sun fully hidden by the Moon, a bright glowing corona, stars visible during the day, and dramatic twilight on the horizon.
whyItMatters: This will be one of the most accessible and longest total solar eclipses in Europe for many decades.
keyFacts: Long duration of totality (over 5 minutes in best locations)
nextOccurrences: The next total solar eclipse with good visibility across Europe is not expected until the 22nd century.
Other total solar eclipses will continue to occur in different parts of the world.

title: Uranus–Neptune conjunction
shortDescription: Uranus and Neptune will appear very close together in the sky — a rare conjunction of the two ice giants.
mainDescription: Uranus and Neptune — the two distant ice giants of the Solar System — will appear unusually close together during a rare planetary conjunction in 2093. Separated by only about one degree in the night sky, the planets will fit comfortably within the same binocular or telescope field of view, creating a sight that few people in history have ever had the opportunity to observe. Because Uranus and Neptune orbit so far from the Sun and move very slowly across the sky, conjunctions between them occur only about once every 172 years. Neither planet is bright enough to be seen with the naked eye under normal conditions, but both will be visible with modest observing equipment. For astronomers, the alignment offers a rare chance to compare the Solar System’s two ice giants side by side — worlds similar in size, yet different in color, atmosphere, and internal structure.
whatYoullSee: Two faint blue-green planets very close to each other when viewed through binoculars or a telescope.
whyItMatters: Such conjunctions between Uranus and Neptune occur only once every 172 years, making it a truly once-in-a-lifetime event for most people.
keyFacts: Visible with binoculars or small telescope
Both planets will be in the constellation Virgo
nextOccurrences: The next Uranus–Neptune conjunction will occur in 2265 (172 years later).

title: Transit of Venus
shortDescription: Venus will pass directly across the face of the Sun, appearing as a small black dot.
mainDescription: Venus will pass directly between Earth and the Sun in 2117, creating one of the rarest predictable astronomical events visible from Earth. During the transit, Venus will appear as a small dark disk slowly crossing the bright face of the Sun over the course of several hours. Unlike a solar eclipse, Venus covers only a tiny portion of the solar surface, but the precision and rarity of the alignment make the event historically and scientifically significant. Transits of Venus occur in a repeating pattern separated by more than a century, making them extraordinarily uncommon within a human lifetime. The previous pair took place in 2004 and 2012, and after the 2117 transit, the next one will not occur until 2125. For centuries, observations of Venus transits played an important role in astronomy, helping scientists refine measurements of the scale of the Solar System and the distance between Earth and the Sun. Because the event involves direct observation of the Sun, proper solar filters will be essential for safe viewing.
whatYoullSee: A tiny black dot (Venus) slowly crossing the disk of the Sun over several hours.
whyItMatters: This is one of the rarest celestial events that can be predicted far in advance.
keyFacts: Occurs in pairs separated by over 100 years
Last transit pair was in 2004 and 2012
Requires solar filter or safe projection method
nextOccurrences: The second transit of the pair will occur on December 8, 2125.
After 2125, the next transit of Venus will not occur until 2247.

title: Second transit of Venus
shortDescription: The second and final transit of Venus in the current pair, occurring just 8 years after the first.
mainDescription: Venus will once again cross directly in front of the Sun in 2125, completing the rare pair of transits that began with the 2117 event. Over the course of several hours, the planet will appear as a small black silhouette moving slowly across the Sun’s bright disk — a precise alignment of orbital motion that occurs only at very specific intervals. Although visually subtle compared to a solar eclipse, transits of Venus are among the rarest predictable astronomical phenomena visible from Earth. These events occur in pairs separated by eight years, but each pair is itself separated by more than a century. After the 2125 transit, the next transit of Venus will not occur until the 23rd century, making this the last opportunity for many generations to witness the phenomenon firsthand. For centuries, Venus transits carried major scientific importance, helping astronomers measure the scale of the Solar System and refine humanity’s understanding of Earth’s place in space.
whatYoullSee: A tiny black dot (Venus) slowly moving across the bright surface of the Sun.
whyItMatters: This completes one of the rarest predictable celestial events, closing a pair that will not repeat for over 100 years.
keyFacts: Occurs 8 years after the first transit
Requires solar filter for safe viewing
nextOccurrences: After 2125, the next transit of Venus will not occur until December 2247.

title: Annular solar eclipse (ring of fire)
shortDescription: The Moon will pass in front of the Sun, creating a spectacular “ring of fire” effect.
mainDescription: The Moon will pass directly in front of the Sun in 2126, creating a striking annular solar eclipse visible across parts of the Pacific, North America, and the Atlantic region. Because the Moon will be slightly farther from Earth than during a total solar eclipse, it will appear too small to completely cover the Sun. Instead, a bright ring of sunlight will remain visible around the Moon’s dark silhouette, producing the distinctive “Ring of Fire” effect that gives annular eclipses their popular name. Although the sky will not become fully dark during annularity, daylight will noticeably dim and the Sun will take on an unusually sharp and dramatic appearance. The event will offer a rare example of the delicate balance between the apparent sizes of the Sun and Moon in Earth’s sky — a coincidence made possible by the geometry of the Earth–Moon system. Because part of the Sun always remains visible, proper solar filters will be required throughout the entire eclipse for safe observation.
whatYoullSee: A bright ring of sunlight surrounding the dark silhouette of the Moon.
whyItMatters: Annular eclipses produce one of the most visually unique and photogenic effects in astronomy.
keyFacts: Moon appears smaller than the Sun
Path crosses the Pacific and parts of North America
nextOccurrences: Annular solar eclipses occur more frequently than total ones, usually every few years somewhere on Earth.

title: Comet Swift–Tuttle return
shortDescription: The parent comet of the Perseid meteor shower will return to the inner Solar System.
mainDescription: Comet Swift–Tuttle will return to the inner Solar System in 2126 after completing its long 132-year orbit around the Sun. Known as the parent body of the annual Perseid meteor shower, the comet is responsible for the streams of dust that create one of Earth’s most famous meteor displays every August. During its return, sunlight will heat the comet’s icy surface, releasing gas and dust that may form a glowing coma and an extended tail visible from Earth. The exact brightness of long-period comets is difficult to predict far in advance, but a comet of Swift–Tuttle’s size has the potential to become visible to the naked eye under dark skies. For future observers, the event will offer a rare opportunity to see the actual object behind the Perseids — a comet that continues to shape one of the most familiar annual events in Earth’s night sky.
whatYoullSee: A comet with a glowing head and possibly a long tail, visible in dark skies.
whyItMatters: It connects the famous Perseid meteor shower with its parent comet, offering a direct link between annual meteors and their origin.
keyFacts: Parent body of the Perseid meteor shower
May become visible to the naked eye
nextOccurrences: Comet Swift–Tuttle will return again around 2259.
